extracted.intended_audience: Citizens and voters of New York; readers engaged in the constitutional ratification debate
extracted.subtask_description: A framework for assessing whether a proposed constitution conforms to republican principles, whether it is federal or national in character, and whether the convention that proposed it was authorized to do so. Includes practical criteria and examples used to defend the new plan against objections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conformity to republican principles
rubrics_metrics.description: A republic is (or should be) 'a government which derives all its powers directly or indirectly from the great body of the people, and is administered by persons holding their offices during pleasure, for a limited period, or during good behavior.' It is essential that power be derived from the great body of society, not an inconsiderable proportion or favored class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sufficient that officers be appointed directly or indirectly by the people and hold their appointments under the tenures described. Examples given: House elected immediately by the people; Senate indirectly; President indirectly; judges by good behavior. Additional proofs of republican complexion: prohibition of titles of nobility and express guaranty of republican form to States.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tenure and mode of appointment as evidence of republicanism
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare the mode of appointment and the length/tenure of offices to state constitutions to judge republican character (e.g., House two-year terms, Senate six years, President four years, judges during good behavior).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use prevailing State constitutions as benchmarks—if the new plan's appointment modes and tenures align with common State practice, this supports its republican character. The text compares the proposed terms with those of South Carolina, Maryland, New York, Virginia, Delaware, etc., to show conformity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative improvement (sufficiency over perfection)
rubrics_metrics.description: A proposed constitution need not be perfect; it is sufficient that it be less imperfect than the existing system it replaces. 'It is not necessary that the former should be perfect; it is sufficient that the latter is more imperfect.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate new proposals relative to the defects of the current system (Confederation). Use practical tradeoffs and examples (brass for silver, a new but not perfect house vs a shattered habitation) to justify adopting a better-but-imperfect plan.

rubrics_metrics.name: Danger of indefinite powers (raising money)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask whether the constitution vests an 'indefinite power to raise money' and whether that is dangerous—compare to the existing Confederation, which also allows requisitions, issuing bills of credit, and borrowing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine whether powers to tax/borrow/emit currency are constrained or indefinite; compare how the present Congress already exercises similar powers. The mere existence of power is not unique to the proposed Constitution if the Confederation permits like powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Danger of indefinite powers (raising troops)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask whether there is an 'indefinite power to raise troops' and whether that is dangerous; note that the Confederation already vests Congress with equivalent military-raising powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the practical checks on troop-raising and whether dependence on States for means renders the power harmless. Consider precedent: the Confederation has given Congress similar authority and has begun to exercise it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concentration/mixing of powers is hazardous
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether different powers of government are intermixed in the same body of men (e.g., treasury and command of the army in same hands) and whether that mixing is unsafe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare to current practice under the Confederation (Congress is a single body holding many federal powers). If the existing system already mixes powers, objections to the new plan on this ground must reconcile that fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bill of Rights question
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether a bill of rights is essential to liberty and whether the absence/presence of such a bill is a decisive objection to the proposed Constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note the Confederation has no bill of rights; weigh whether the new plan's protections are adequate despite this. The page raises the question but also points to other checks and comparisons with the existing system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foundation test: federal vs national (where assent/ratification originates)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the Constitution is federal or national by examining on what foundation it is established: federal if founded on the assent of the people acting as distinct States (each State's supreme authority), national if resulting from the majority of the whole people of the Union.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key indicators: whether ratification requires unanimous assent of the several States or a majority of the people; whether the act is expressed as the assent of separate States rather than an aggregate nation. The paper emphasizes that the proposed plan results from assent of States and is therefore federal in foundation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources of ordinary powers: who they derive from
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide federal vs national character by examining the sources of ordinary powers: e.g., House of Representatives derives powers directly from the people (national feature); Senate derives from the States (federal feature); the executive is from a compound source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze each branch: representation proportional to people vs equality of States; consider how votes for president are allocated (compound ratio). Use comparisons to State constitutions for tenure and appointment modes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operation of powers: on political bodies or individuals
rubrics_metrics.description: Judge whether powers operate on political bodies (federal) or on individual citizens (national). If powers routinely act directly on individuals, that indicates national operation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concrete cases to test this: trial of controversies where States are parties (federal), versus cases like capture, piracy, post office, coinage, trade with Indians, land grants, courts-martial where the government's powers act on individuals—these indicate national operation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extent of powers (scope/jurisdiction) as federal vs national indicator
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the government's jurisdiction is an indefinite supremacy over all persons/things (national) or limited to certain enumerated objects with residuary sovereignty left to States (federal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the plan leaves unenumerated cases to States and confines the general government to enumerated powers, that supports a federal character in extent. Consider whether local authorities remain independent within their spheres.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mode of amendment as federal vs national indicator
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine the authority and procedure for making amendments: national would place ultimate authority in a majority of the people; federal would require concurrence of each State. The proposed plan requires more than a mere majority and computes proportion by States, mixing both characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the amendment mechanism tilts toward national (majority-of-people) or federal (unanimous or state-concurrence). The plan's mixed mode (some state-weighted thresholds, less than unanimous) shows neither purely national nor purely federal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convention mandate: scope of authority given by commissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine the convention's authority by inspecting the commissions and recommendatory acts (Annapolis recommendation, Congress's resolute calling to 'revise the Articles' and make 'alterations and provisions' to render government 'adequate to the exigencies of the Union').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List the concrete objects authorized: to devise 'such further provisions as shall appear necessary,' to report alterations and provisions to render the Constitution adequate. Use these textual sources to deduce whether framing a national and adequate government was within the convention's mandate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule of construction for interpreting commissions (ends over means)
rubrics_metrics.description: When commissions contain expressions that cannot all be reconciled, give meaning to every part where possible; where they cannot be made to coincide, allow the less important part to give way to the more important—'the means should be sacrificed to the end, rather than the end to the means.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply this hermeneutic when evaluating alleged overreach: prioritize the ultimate objective (establishing an adequate national government) over narrow textual limits when the ends clearly demanded substantial reform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish authorized alterations from a transmutation of government
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether proposed changes fall within authorized 'alterations and further provisions' or amount to a full TRANSMUTATION of the government that exceeds the convention's commission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require explicit boundaries showing which innovations are within 'alterations' and which are usurpations. The text calls on critics to 'mark the boundary between authorized and usurped innovations.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity/duty can supply defects of regular authority
rubrics_metrics.description: If the convention lacked strict legal authority, consider whether urgent public necessity and duty (the crisis and public expectation) justified informal or unauthorized propositions to provide an adequate government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look to historical context: widespread conviction of crisis, prior public opinion, examples of prior assumptions by Congress and local actors, and the impracticability of perfect formal commission in times of emergency as justifications for taking bold action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use precedent and practical conduct of government as evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate the practical acts of existing bodies (e.g., Congress administering western lands, forming new States, appointing officers without clear authority) as evidence of existing dangers or as precedents that affect the assessment of a proposed plan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the present government has exceeded its formal powers in practice (creating a large independent revenue fund, taking on territorial administration, etc.), that fact should weigh in favor of accepting reform that provides regular powers commensurate to governmental objects to avoid dissolution or usurpation.
